PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext: Today this House is signally honoured by the presence in the Speaker's Gallery of Lai Bahadur Shastri, Prime Minister of India.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
This is the first visit to Canada by Prime Minister Shastri, who is such a worthy successor to the late and beloved Prime Minister Nehru. We welcome him as a fellow parliamentarian and as the elected leader of the world's largest democracy.
The Prime Minister of our great Commonwealth partner is a man of the people, a man of peace. At the early age of 16 he became a follower of Mahatma Ghandi and played a courageous part in the struggle for national freedom. Since then he has been a leading figure in India's constructive and successful quest for self determination and has served his people with integrity, competence and humility. The election of Lai Bahadur to the highest office within the gift of his people demonstrates very strikingly the effectiveness of the democratic process in India.
Relations between India and Canada have always been close and cordial. We have very much in common. We are both countries that stretch from sea to sea. It was in the search for a short route to India that our country was first discovered, and our original inhabitants still carry the honoured name of Indians. On the world scene, as fellow members of the Commonwealth of Nations we have worked together and have shared the same aspirations for a world at peace. In the management of our own affairs we have each followed the parliamentary process as common inheritors of the British tradition of democracy.
Today in Canada we are striving to meet and master problems of national unity that are the product of 400 short years in which men and women of two languages and two
cultures have lived side by side. Surely we can take heart from the example of India- a multilingual, multiracial society, an amalgam of many religions and cultures, with a history extending over so many centuries. Her very substantial accomplishments, in the face of so many hardships, are surely an example to all the world.
We welcome you, Sir. We honour you as the leader of a great and historic nation whose future progress will be a major determinant in the ultimate survival of democracy and peace among the nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, in accordance with a commitment I gave the Leader of the Opposition some days ago I wish to advise the House of certain decisions which have been made about the future use and form of the social insurance number card.
It will be recalled that this card was first issued last year in connection with unemployment insurance, and was designed to provide the same numbering system for the

June 11, 1965
Social Insurance Card Canada Pension Plan. Some Provincial Governments have expressed an interest in the possible use of the same numbers and cards in connection with other programs. This clearly would be a considerable convenience to the public. It means, however, that the card should be one suitable for use in connection with programs under the authority of Provincial as well as Federal legislation. It also makes the durability of the card even more important. The Government therefore intends to introduce a plastic card.
Second, in order to provide a national symbol equally appropriate for programs under either Federal or Provincial jurisdiction, the card has been redesigned with a maple leaf superimposed by the word "Canada" in place of the coat of arms which is a distinctively Federal symbol and therefore not the most suitable for Provincial use. The card in this new form will be suitable for many possible uses besides the most urgent one which, of course, is for both Federal and Provincial pension plans.

speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING COMPULSORY BREATHALIZER TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose
of this Bill is to reduce the death and accident toll taken by traffic. It would seek to do this by enacting legislation to control the impaired driver. Statistics show that in recent years one third of the road accidents in Canada involve persons who have been drinking. The Bill which I put forward incorporates proposals made by the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Highway Safety Council. Specifically it would amend the Criminal Code to make compulsory breathalizer tests for determining blood alcohol levels.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
If I may have the attention of the House for just a moment I should like to make a short statement.
I am sure this House will be interested to know that I have accepted an invitation from the Speaker of the British House of Commons to attend, in London, a conference of Speakers from the 21 member nations of the Commonwealth. Following that conference I have been asked to participate in a ceremony at Westminster to mark the 700th anniversary of the Parliament of Simon de Montfort and the 750th anniversary of Magna Carta.
I propose as well to journey to Geneva for discussions with Mr. Andre de Blonay, Secretary-General of the Inter-Parliamentary

June 11, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry Bureau, concerning the annual meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Union to be held in Ottawa in September of this year.
I plan also to make a brief visit to Paris to discuss with M. Chaban-Delmas, President of the French National Assembly, ways and means of strengthening the links between Parliamentarians of our two countries. I expect to return to Ottawa the week end of June 25.
During my absence, with the leave of the House, the Deputy Speaker, the hon. Member for Stormont, would occupy the Chair. I ask leave of the House to engage in the service of the House overseas.

maintopic: PROCEDURE

speechtext:
I appreciate that the motion is debatable, and I appreciate also the fact that we are working under a guillotine imposed by the House of Commons some time ago so that the discussion of this report, plus the other matters before us in connection with the rules, have to be finished by five o'clock. I should like to say this, that the report which has been brought back to the House, as the report itself states, was adopted by the Committee on division and is not a unanimous opinion from that Committee.

I intend to speak very briefly in order to give to the backbenchers of this House, who are almost in revolt against limitations of time that are now being imposed in the House and who have apparently discovered that the major changes in the rules are striking at the freedom of the backbenchers, an opportunity to speak. On the other hand, I realize that if there is a vote on this report it will be an open vote since the rules affect every single Member individually. It is not a case of the Government versus the Opposition. I presume if there is a vote we will be able to observe the independence expressed by various Members of this House without the whips compelling them to do something they do not wish to do.
I just want to say this, Sir. Now that we are reaching the end of this revision of the rules and procedures, the most extensive revision since 1955, I hope there will be an appropriate pause for a year or two until we see the effects of the changes rather than trying to press on with some more changes. It has become obvious that once you start making changes in the rules and procedures of this House you discover problems that were not evident before. What is coming out of this major change in the rules and procedures is an increase in the power of the executive, which already was too great and should have been diminished. The private Members of this House are beginning to realize that, but rather too late in the day.
The second thing that comes out of it is a restriction on the freedom of speech so far as the Opposition are concerned, and the time they may devote to matters of public interest can be seriously restricted. This is a dangerous move and may have bad effects in the future.
The third matter that comes out of the study of the proposed changes is that shackles are being placed on the private Members of this House by the private Members themselves. They failed, a few days ago, to pay close attention to the speeches that were made on this subject. Only yesterday did they appear to awaken to the fact that they were encouraging the executive to put shackles on the private Members. We heard quite a bit about the advantages that accrue to those who are on the front benches and the disadvantages to those who are somewhat further removed from the aisle. I hope today the backbenchers will assert their rights by their vote and restrain the Government from the imposition of a second method of closure.

They have one on the books now and they are putting on another one.
Quite a bit of this has come about because of the composition of the present executive. Several of the most prominent members of the treasury benches have not gone through that orderly progression from the back row to the front row. It is a rather slow process, as some of us have found out, but it has its advantages. You get the point of view of the private Member which a person who is catapulted into the front row does not get.
The present Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport-I will not mention all the others-were catapulted into the front row. The Prime Minister entered the front row, I presume, when he entered the House, and the Minister of Transport got into the second row from the front, which was too far advanced a position for him at that time anyway. Nevertheless, there was the unusual progression from outside of the House of Commons right to the treasury benches. These gentlemen did not receive the training that I believe a parliamentarian should get; that is, to start at the curtains in the back row and gradually move forward. In this way an hon. Member has an idea of the penalties that fall upon the less prominent Members of the House of Commons as they sit in the back row and then gradually move forward.
I put in a plea ten days ago on behalf of the backbenchers, and I return to that subject now. People come into this House in the same way, by the votes within a constituency. There is a great equality at election time when you are standing for election. Every person is in the same position, in that it is the votes of the people in the constituency that move him into the House of Commons. When he gets into the House of Commons he finds everybody there is equal, but some are more equal than others. He discovers, slowly and painfully when he sits in the back row, that he is to be seen and not heard unless the whip of the party, acting under instructions, discovers that a debate requires somebody to carry it on. Then the backbencher is a very useful person. I have been all through this, and I realize what it is.
It is nice to have a backbencher around to vote, very nice to have him around to maintain a quorum in the House. Under the rules now it will be the backbencher who will be here during the lunch hour because the people on the front benches will have to go to have their meals. I realize that when you are in the back benches you must not interfere with the front benchers when they are making the

House of Commons Procedures lead off speeches on some subject. After they have made their speeches, then the backbencher is called, the subject having been fairly well exhausted by those previous utterances of the front benches. The backbencher is asked often to make a 30 or 40 minute speech because one of the frontbenchers who is away wants to come back the next day and contribute to the debate, so it must be kept open. I have been through that on many occasions. This goes back a good many years.
This is the function of the backbencher. He is a very useful person on occasion. When there is a limited debate, when closure has been applied, it is only the frontbenchers who are to be heard, the people who will speak for their party and express the opinion of the party. The backbencher is just to sit and listen and when the time comes, to vote.
This is the most difficult position the backbencher occupies in this House under the changes in the rules that have been brought forward. The first major change came in 1955 when a restriction was placed on the length of the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and the Budget debate. Backbenchers were then squeezed out because there was not sufficient available time for them to participate in debates. Now they are contributing to squeezing themselves out further, and their function in Parliament will be less prominent than it has been in the past. [DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
In the report presented to us today a sop is thrown out to the backbencher, in that on a closure motion which gives one day for debate on third reading there can be an extension of four hours beyond normal closing time if backbenchers who have not been heard, but still want to get something on the record, suggest to the Speaker that their names be placed on the list of speakers to be called. The extra four hours will be granted to them to express themselves but each individual will be limited to 20 minutes, so that only 12 may be heard; and if 40 others wish to be heard they will be chopped off.
This is what I call the anti-whip amendment, because it gives the backbenchers who are not in good standing with their whips, who cannot get on their party list of speakers, an opportunity to go direct to Mr. Speaker on the last day of a closed debate and get the opportunity to be heard.
I pity the backbenchers in the future. I regret they have not aroused themselves in large numbers on this occasion, and have not seen that the executive is grasping more
2262	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures power. They have not seen that the backbencher is being relegated to an even more inferior position than he has occupied in the past. He is now being asked to put the Shackles on himself, to fasten the ball and chain on his own foot so that his activities in this Chamber will be reduced.
Much of what we are seeking would have been achieved by extending the hours of sitting from 25J to 33 hours per week. This would have made the necessary provision for shortening a session, as some desire, and giving more Members the opportunity to speak. But we have gone further than that because the Government insists on the closure rule and backbenchers are being asked to confer this great power on the executive.
With a limit on this debate, with the guillotine not quite as sharp as it was yesterday, its edge a bit blunted, but with it ready to fall at five o'clock this evening, I now relinquish the floor to the backbenchers of the House of Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all enjoyed the delightful touches of irony with which the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre has regaled us with during the speech he has just terminated under his own voluntary guillotine.
The hon. Member has rightly pointed out that the report of the special committee consisting of nine Members of the House was agreed to on division. I rise, as a member of the committee who supported the report, to support the motion for its adoption, and like the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre I shall try to keep my remarks brief. However,
I feel one fundamental point should be emphasized once more.
In the main the business of the House of Commons consists of two things. We must have the chance to speak, the right to discuss all the matters that are brought before us; and second, we must have the right to reach decisions. The whole problem in parliamentary procedure is to find a balance between these two propositions.
This is not the first time Parliament has attempted to find that balance. When limitations were put on the length of time a Member could speak, that was part of the attempt. In 1955 when certain debates, such as on the Address, the Budget and supply motions, were limited, that was another attempt to achieve that balance. What we are now proposing is that that step be carried a

DEBATES	June 11, 1965
bit further, that there be arrangements Whereby the House itself can come to agreement that certain other debates be given a time limit so that certain items can be concluded and the House can get on to other matters.
I think the House generally believes this is the wise and responsible thing to do. I believe the people of Canada support us in our contention that we should organize our parliamentary year, which includes planning the use of our parliamentary time. Therefore I am not disturbed by the manner in which the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre tries to suggest, as he has done so often, that we are extending the principle of closure. That is not an accurate description of the rule we are now discussing. All he is doing is arguing by assertion.
The one thing the country has the right to expect us to do is to organize our work better, and it is on that basis that we support the principle of the allocation of time. Indeed, we have been urging for some considerable time that this be adopted. You, M!r. Deputy Speaker, will recall serving with others and with me as members of a subcommittee on procedure last session when we worked on this problem and came up with draft orders along this very line, which in fact had wide support.
When this matter was discussed earlier in the House arguments arose over the wording of the proposal for an allocation of time order. As a result the matter was referred to a special committee of nine Members of the House, and it is the report of that committee which we now have before us.
The hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre referred briefly to the one change of substance that our committee has recommended, and I should like to refer to it also, but I do so as a supporter of the proposed change. May I point out that the rule as sent to the committee provided for certain conditions under which allocation limits could be set. It established a certain set of minimum provisions under which, if a Minister was moving a time allocation order without the support of the business committee, the least he could ask for would be two days on second reading, two days in Committee of the Whole, and one day on third reading. Some people thought this would be the pattern in all cases, but that does not follow at all. The Business Committee itself may recommend shorter or
June 11, 1965

longer periods, and even a Minister may recommend longer periods.
In the case of a money bill, the minimum time possible is six days; for in addition to those five days on the bill itself there is the one day already provided for discussion of the resolution preceding the bill, and when a Minister moves a time allocation order there can be an additional day's debate on that motion.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
We must also face the fact that even though some of us are opposed to the provision to extend the hours by sitting from six to eight, nevertheless that provision has been passed. The result is that each day will be longer, so the possibility of six full days of debate on a money measure adds up to quite a few more hours than would have been the case in six days of debate under the former rules. Having in mind the amount of time taken in a parliament such as Westminster, I maintain we are not being unreasonable in giving our support to the principle of time allocation translated into these specific terms.
Let me come now to the one substantial change which the committee of nine has proposed. I wish there had been an opportunity to print these recommendations as an appendix to Hansard, in order that all hon. Members might have before them the substance of the proposal. That, however, is a matter for the Minister rather than for me. What we have proposed is that when third reading of a bill takes place under a time allocation, whether it is the one day minimum or whether it is any length of time that the business committee may have recommended, at ten o'clock on the last day of the time allocated for third reading it shall be possible for the debate to be extended. We have made this recommendation because we feel the appeals made by backbenchers are legitimate. We are not trying to protect the right of filibuster, the right to prevent a decision from being reached. We are saying there are occasions when Members representing constituencies rightfully feel they should have a chance to speak come what may. So we have recommended that on this final day Mr. Speaker shall have the authority to extend the time available up to an additional four hours. We have recommended that during this four hour period speeches shall be limited to 20 minutes and that speakers shall be drawn from among those who have notified Mr. Speaker that they wish to get on his list and who have given their notice at least one hour before the normal adjournment time. If 22620-145
House of Commons Procedures the House were under an allocation of time order on third reading, at eight o'clock on the last day Members who wanted to speak would notify Mr. Speaker. If the number was small enough to enable all of them to "get on" by ten o'clock, that would be fine. But if there should be too many, Mr. Speaker has the right to continue the sitting for a further four hours and he will choose the speakers from among those who have notified him of their wish to speak.
We have also provided that during this four hour period there shall be no further amendments or subamendments. In other words we are providing for the genuine case of the backbencher who feels he must get his word into the debate, despite the fact that he has not managed to do so. We have also provided that if during the extended period, say between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., there is a call for a vote the vote shall not be taken at that time, providing five members so request, but that it be postponed until the next sitting day when it will, of necessity, be taken as the first item under Government orders, without further debate.
I can see that we might have done better. We might have made the period longer. We might have set no final limit. But I suggest this represents a distinct improvement compared with the proposed standing order as we first took it under consideration in the committee of nine. I put it to the House that we have done a bit more toward achieving a balance between the right of Members to speak and the right of Parliament to reach a point at which a decision is made.
I believe it was a good idea for this proposed standing order to be referred to the special committee. I believe the special committee has come back with a good report. I am sorry it is not unanimous, but it is the report of the committee and I hope Members generally will acknowledge that it should be supported and that it should become an order of the House, as provided in the report itself, for the balance of this session and for the next session of this Parliament, subject to whatever decision the House may make at that time.
Mr. Speaker, I have pleasure in supporting the motion for the adoption of this report.

I, too, would like to support the report which has come back from the special committee of nine in connection with the second paragraph of the resolution before us.
I find it strange that an argument can be advanced that this in some way is likely to
2264	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures infringe on the rights and privileges of backbenchers. I say it seems strange, having in mind the fact that I have not heard anyone complaining in this House that the arrangements made for the debate on the Budget and the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, each limited in extent, constitute an infringement of the rights and privileges of backbenchers.
We know that even if all the provisions contained in the new standing order 15 were used it would be impossible for a Government to limit a debate to less than one day on the resolution, in the case of a bill, two days for second reading, two days in committee after second reading and one day plus an overtime period of four hours on third reading. I would also draw to the attention of the House the fact that in addition to these six days there is also a one day debate which can be demanded on the motion to impose these rules. Therefore, every time this Standing Order 15A is used, provision will be made for an amount of time to be spent on one single piece of legislation at least equal to that which is available for discussion of the Speech from the Throne, a discussion which is, I suggest, of far greater magnitude inasmuch as it embraces the whole of the Government's legislative program for the session.
Indeed, even more time will be allowed taking into account the extra hours which will be available each day. At present the debate on the Budget is limited to six sitting days of about five hours each day. In other words it is limited to about 30 hours. This debate on the Budget involves the whole of the Government's fiscal policy for the year. Yet even should the Minister use every one of the provisions of this standing order he cannot provide for less time on a single piece of legislation than is now available to backbenchers to deal with the Government's whole fiscal policy for the year.
I cannot, therefore, accept the argument that this proposed standing order is in any way an infringement or a curtailment of the right of backbenchers to participate in debates. What it does is this. It provides that we shall move on from one piece of legislation to another within reasonable time limits. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the most effective form of closure we have witnessed in this House is the abuse of these open-ended debates which prevents us moving from one piece of legislation to another.

If a businessman handled his affairs the way the House of Commons handles its business, I believe he soon would be bankrupt.
The debate dealt mostly with paragraph 7 of section 15A of resolution No. 15 concerning the limitation of debates. Mr. Speaker, earlier in this debate I suggested

The reason I made this suggestion was that I felt the possibility of a debate being extended all through the evening would be so unpleasant to Members on the front benches, and other Members in the House, that a real incentive would be provided to recognize the rights of private Members. It would retain, in other words, a negotiating position for the private Member. The limitations which have been placed upon the extension of debate are such as to completely destroy that particular reason for my suggestion. In other words the private Member's negotiating position has been destroyed completely, and the amendment really does not improve his negotiating position at all.
The first of the three limitations to which I refer is that the extension of four hours only applies on third reading. This is, of course, after the principle of the bill has been approved. Second reading is the time when the principle of the bill should be debated; so if there is any merit at all in giving the private Member a right to be heard, surely it should be on second reading and not on third reading.

The other two limitations are matters upon which I would be interested in hearing from those hon. Members who have spoken in favour of this amendment. I realize that arguments can be put forward in favour of these particular limitations, but I suggest the real reason for them is to dispense with the necessity of anyone being here during the extended debate. At least, Mr. Speaker, this is one possible effect of these two limitations, because I must not impute motives. They will make it unnecessary for members of the front bench or, indeed, for Members in all parts of the House, to be present while the private Members try to make their points. The effect is to completely destroy the negotiating position which I hoped the backbencher would retain with an extended debate.
It has been pointed out that this measure will be applied on a trial basis. I think it is a very good thing that it is on a trial basis. But since it is on this basis I would have thought that those who introduced it could have afforded to be generous in protecting the rights of backbenchers rather than restricting them. If they had been generous and had given more protection to the rights of backbenchers, perhaps it would have been found after the trial period that legislation was not being filibustered after all. It seems to me rather pessimistic on their part to assume that they must limit the rights of backbenchers to the extent that they have, in order to make certain there shall be no unduly extended debate.
I think most of us are very happy with many of the amendments that have been made; we think they will improve the procedure of the House. However, Mr. Speaker, it does seem to me that since this particular rule is being adopted on a trial basis, more generous measures should have been taken to make sure that the negotiating position of the private, back bench Member was retained.
I would ask the House Leader, the President of the Privy Council, when he speaks to tell us what will happen, for example, to the rights of the backbencher in view of these limitations if there is no quorum in the House. Will the right of the backbencher be completely destroyed? I made a number of suggestions when I spoke a few days ago in this debate. I believe that any one of them could have been adopted and they would have preserved the rights of the backbencher while at the same time permitting the Government to get its legislation through without undue delay. I suggest that even at this late date some improvements could be made in this particular rule.

Mr. Chairman, last evening when ten o'clock rolled around I was commenting on section 6 of the resolution regarding the rules and procedures of the House.
I was pointing out that while I had not intended to comment on this recommendation of the Government, I felt impelled to rise in view of some comments which had been made by the hon. Member for Prince Albert last Tuesday when he was speaking on the rules and procedures, and at which time direct reference was made to myself. You may remember that I recalled that on May 28 I had asked the Minister of Justice a question about whether his Department or the Cabinet had ever given consideration to making it illegal for mass communication media to mention names of accused before they are convicted. As reported at page 1769 1 remarked:
Personally, I do not believe they should be mentioned by name until a conviction has been registered-
Yesterday I indicated that the Minister had given a straightforward answer. His reply was:
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this...is one of the questions which I have under very serious consideration...
But there is also such a thing as respect for the freedom of the individual and in the case of juveniles the regulation already exists in the Criminal Code that their names must not be disclosed in the papers. Surely this is not an interference with the freedom of the press.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I commented last night that a straightforward question on a simple point of practice in the mass communication field had been blown out of all proportion, by people with financial interests in the mass communication field, into an interpretation that this is an attack on the freedom of the press. I have never seen such exaggeration in such a short period of time. I rise to point out that this question is not dead and it will not be killed. The hon. Member for Prince Albert in speaking last Tuesday made the statement:
-it was only as a result of publicity that this announcement found its way into the limbo of forgotten things.
When he refers to the announcement he means the remarks passed by the Minister of Justice in reply to my question. I can assure you here and now that this matter has not found its way into the limbo of forgotten
June 11. 1965

House of Commons Procedures things. It is quite interesting to me that the hon. Member for Lafontaine, who sits to my left, on numerous occasions in the past has introduced private bills on this very point, and right now in your binder for private bills, Mr. Chairman, you will find Bill No. C-90 in which the hon. Member for Lafontaine is seeking to amend the Criminal Code so that there will be a restriction of publication of proceedings. He does not say the elimination of the publication of proceedings; he talks about the restriction of publication of proceedings; and in the explanatory notes it is stated that the purpose of the proposed amendments are:
(2) to eliminate the unfortunate results of judicial errors.
Included in that is the case of people being accused of offences of which they are later acquitted or found not guilty, and to prevent their names being dragged all over the universe because they have been falsely accused in the first place. I commend the integrity of the Member for Lafontaine in getting behind this bill of his, which he has been urging in season and out of season for some time.
Further down on this side of the House we find the hon. Member for Norfolk. He has on the order paper private Member's notice of motion No. 15, introduced in this House on April 6, long before I asked the question on May 28. The hon. Member for Norfolk under private Members' notices of motions moves:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Criminal Code so that an accused person who is eventually found not guilty-
In other words, so as to provide that a person who has been unjustly kept in custody and is afterwards acquitted may be paid his costs, expenses and compensation. I bring forward these examples to show you that the thinking of the nation is along the lines that accused people who are subsequently found not guilty are not being treated fairly in this country of ours today, despite all the uproar in the press about freedom of the press.
The hon. Member for Norfolk is not in the Chamber, but I will take the liberty of saying to you that he is interested in this question because of comments that have been made to him over the years by a Judge in western Ontario who has commented on more than one occasion privately on the injustice to accused persons who are later found not guilty, having their names dragged all over the front pages of the newspapers, blasted over the radio waves and exposed on television screens when they have done no wrong.

The Judge gives a certain example of a man who was held for two years in a county jail and was later acquitted of the charge. No compensation was given to the man, and his name was broadcast all over the countryside simply because an accusation had been made against him.
Last Saturday an article appeared in the Montreal Star following the comments that had been made in this House by the Minister of Justice and the right hon. Prime Minister, both of whom I commend for their statements and attitude on this question. The article, by one Leslie Roberts, in the centre contains this phrase:
The disjointed discussion of press freedom in the House may be a tempest in a teapot.
First of all, I wish Mr. Roberts would get this matter straight. There has been no disjointed discussion of press freedom in this House. There may have been a disjointed discussion of the freedom of the individuals in this House, but there has been no discussion of press freedom. The same writer refers to the Prime Minister's remarks of June 1 as being "an odd intervention". I personally wish to commend the Prime Minister for having answered the hon. Member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue, who on June 1 directed a question to the Minister of Justice.
I have already stated that the Minister of Justice gave a straightforward answer on May 28, one that any man of compassion and religious convictions will support wholeheartedly, when he said that the right of the individual, the freedom of the individual, takes priority over freedom of the press. speechtext:
This is the clause, I assume, that actually sets up the new nomenclature of the committees. I have an amendment to propose and in order to relate my remarks to this amendment I may say it will simply be to add after paragraph (u) an additional one, to be called paragraph (v), on Delegated Authority. In support of this amendment I want to refer to the first statement made by the Prime Minister when he was speaking in the House on March 18 of this year on this question of the Committees system. He used these words as they appear at page 12544 of Hansard, after having dealt with the increasing strength of the Executive and the weakness of the legislative branch of our Government:
This is a situation which has occupied the attention of all students of democratic parliamentary institutions in recent years, because with the executive you have not only the cabinet but you have behind the cabinet, a growing body of expert
June 11, 1965

House of Commons Procedures officialdom which is inevitably becoming more and more important as government becomes increasingly complex.
Later, he said:
Could we strengthen the legislature by deepening and broadening the committee structure? There are some recommendations in this report which, X believe, when implemented may well have this effect. I hope so.
The right hon. gentleman was referring to the 18th report, I believe, of the committee on procedure. However, when the right hon. gentleman was speaking on the debate which initiated this particular discussion, he did not go as far as he had previously. He then said, in response to a question, that he did not believe a Standing Committee on Delegated Authority was necessary, and he stated two reasons. In the first instance, he said, there is consideration being given to setting up a Royal Commission to inquire into the necessity for an ombudsman. Second, he thought the committees, as constructed and set up by this particular section we are discussing, would provide an opportunity to examine into the very dangerous situation which prompted me to move this amendment. I refer to the very increasing extent to which Government, particularly the Executive Branch of the Government, is operating with the aid of Orders in Council. I cannot accept this statement by the Prime Minister.
In the first place, if a Royal Commission does recommend the establishment of an ombudsman, and if in its infinite wisdom Parliament does decide such an officer is required, it is my submission, as a result of evidence given by the New Zealand ombudsman and as a result of discussions that have taken place in committee with an ombudsman, that without a Parliamentary Committee to which he can bring his recommendations and the grievances which are brought to his attention, he is in a very invidious position. I am not going to add any more because it is not pertinent, but I have quoted these observations to stress the importance of this question, in answer to the Prime Minister's objection to setting up a Committee on Delegated Authority. The experience in connection with ombudsmen has been that they are unable to obtain action in respect of grievances brought to their attention unless there is a committee of this nature to deal with them. I submit this is an ample answer to the Prime Minister.
Then, so far as the committees which we have now are concerned, it is my submission that these committees will concern themselves almost exclusively with the question of esti-

mates and legislation which will come before them. These will be the primary functions. There is no question about it. I submit that a committee which would have the opportunity to deal with the issue of delegated authority, particularly the effect of Orders in Council and improper action taken under Orders in Council, is a very essential part of the parliamentary system at this time.
I am not going to say anything more than that, because time is short and there are a lot of other matters to be dealt with. I urge the Government to give most serious consideration to this particular issue. I think this is one of the most important parts of the rule changes, the establishment of a new form of these committees. If we fail to carryout the ancillary step of having a Committee on Delegated Authority, we are not meeting out responsibilities at this time.

speechtext:
Fine. Like my colleague, I was very surprised that this suggested committee had not been included in the Government's proposals. The purpose of such a committee is self-evident.
No committee on estimates has the powers to take a ministry through its delegated legislation. It has no power to go through the Orders in Council passed by the Privy Council, to see that powers have not been exceeded in cases where, for example, the Governor in Council has been granted powers to make regulations. The committee should have power to see that those regulations are not back-dated prior to the legislation granting the powers, and that no regulatory body is empowered to incur expenses which it has no right to incur.
The pattern of Government in this country, as in others, has grown bigger and bigger and become much more complicated. I cannot agree with the proposition of the Prime Minister that a Royal Commission may be set up-mark you, may be set up-to look into the establishment of an ombudsman. I do not think an ombudsman can put his nose into everything on a voluntary basis. He may act on a complaint, but he is not a general review officer of Government activity.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext: Would the hon. Member not agree that the Prime Minister, in dealing with this subject and explaining why the committee was not proposed, went further in dealing with the subject of an ombudsman and went on to discuss the whole question of administrative tribunals?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
That may be so, but I am not taken with this argument about an ombudsman, because I do not think such an official would accomplish anything of this nature. What Parliament is concerned with is that the carte blanche powers it has granted to the Governor in Council, or to some board, are not exceeded. This is a fundamental feature of the examination of the activities of the Government, that Parliament, through an all-party committee, may review the regulations and pertinent Orders in Council that have been passed. At the moment we are not in a position to do so.
For that reason I think such a committee would benefit the Government because, if the Government comes through such an examination cleanly, it can be satisfied its administration is good. It would remove any suggestion that there has been some excess, and from the point of view of the Opposition
June 11, 1965

House of Commons Procedures there is always the chance that peradventure some excess has been committed.
I am sorry the Government did not see fit to be as reform minded and as drastic as the Committee on Procedure in this regard. I know it will be a big job to staff the committee structure, but on the other hand I do not think a Committee on Delegated Legislation would need to sit year around. Perhaps for the first year it might; but after that it would probably operate for relatively short periods of time.
The President of the Privy Council mentioned administrative tribunals. These have to deal with the relationship between the public and the Government. A Committee on Delegated Legislation would look into the relationship between Parliament and the Government, and the powers granted to Government by Parliament.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The two things are entirely different and therefore, with the greatest respect to the Prime Minister, let me say I do not think his arguments were pertinent to the question. I therefore solicit the support of Members on all sides of the House. This was put forward in the committee in the true spirit of non-partisanship. It was one of the strongest recommendations made, and I heartily commend it to all hon. Members and invite their acceptance of it.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
I am interested in the amendment put forward this afternoon and more specifically in the terms in which it is put forward. I say this because when the committee on procedure made its report- and I regret I do not have that report here with me at the moment-the language used in dealing with this subject was perhaps not as clear as that which has been used today. The report itself raises a much broader subject than the particular one of delegated authority. I note that in discussing this question today the two hon. gentlemen concerned confined themselves to the question of an examination of the use of authority delegated by legislation. They did this very specifically and very clearly, if I may say so. There is undoubtedly a problem developing in this field as it concerns modern legislative bodies. This arises from the very nature of the increase in Government regulatory legislation of one sort or another; there is increasing delegation of authority and an increasing need for vigilance to ensure that an administrative body does not exceed its authority.

Regrettably, as I say-and I believe that if hon. Members would look at this report they would agree with me-the language used by the committee in this case did not express the proposal clearly. I have spent a great deal of time upon the report. I wish I had it here, because it dealt, in essence, with a much broader subject, and, if I may say so without offending anybody-especially as this is sometimes one of my own shortcomings-the recommendation is not as precise in its language as it might have been. I hope the author will not take offence at that remarks; I do think a review of it, now, would illustrate the point I have in mind.
As to the remarks made in the reference by the Prime Minister to this subject of an ombudsman, it is certainly not my view, nor I believe his view, that it is the function of an ombudsman to check on the improper use of delegated authority. It is not any part of his function, although he may, by the nature of his work, be called upon to deal with the point incidentally. If the ombudsman were to point out an abuse or excessive use of delegated authority, it would be incidental to his work rather than a direct part of his responsibility.
But where the possibility of abuse of delegated authority lies is largely with administrative tribunals, and this was the point of the Prime Minister's remarks. A Commission to enquire into administrative tribunals is being set up, and this is the root of the explanation why a Standing Committee was not provided for.
It will be reoalled that the question of administrative tribunals was not dealt with in the Glasseo Commission report. Work on this was started and then discontinued. There is, as I believe hon. Members will agree, a real need for an examination of this subject generally. I think lawyers in all the law associations I know of across this country have agreed on such a need. It seems to me it would be wrong on the one hand to have a standing committee of the House of Commons dealing with the subject of delegated authority at the same time as a commission was dealing with administrative tribunals. The commission will presumably be asked to make recommendations as to what should be done by way of safeguards in this field. Suppose the two bodies were sitting concurrently-the commission and the committee-one can imagine the difficulties which would arise if the commission were to recommend that the Parliamentary committee be discontinued as ineffec-
June 11. 1965	COMMONS
tive. It would surely not be a good idea to have the two bodies sitting at the same time.
There is one other consideration which entered into the decision not to include this committee-
I see the hon. Member for Edmonton West has a question he wants to ask.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext: I wonder whether the President of the Privy Council would not agree there is a fundamental distinction between the functions of a committee and the functions of an administrative tribunal which does not take the annual volume of regulations, and so on, and review them and declare them on a hypothetical basis to be ultra vires, for instance. An administrative tribunal will deal with those matters brought before it on appeal by citizens or as a result of certain legal steps which might be taken by municipal or Government bodies. Those are administrative tribunals. No administrative tribunal exists, I suggest, which would take note of all the delegated legislation and the regulations made under it and review them. And this is the purpose of the committee.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
I quite agree as to the difference between a committee and a commission, but I want to point out that one of the large areas in which there may be abuse, if there is abuse, is likely to be abuse of delegated authority by administrative tribunals. It seems unrealistic when investigating this matter through a commission to have a committee investigating this and other aspects of delegated authority at the same time. That is my point.
The other important factor which entered into the decision not to include this new standing committee is this: It will be seen from the old Standing Order No. 65 that there were some 14 standing committees. In this present revision of House procedures we have proposed 21 standing committees. Hon. Members who examine the list will notice the reference to forestry and rural development for the first time. They will see there is a new Standing Committee on Broadcasting and Films, an important new field. There is a Committee on Crown Corporations. Over the past 10 or 15 years there has been a constant demand for a Standing Committee on Crown Corporations for reasons which I need not elaborate here, except perhaps to say that if they do not get a direct vote in the estimates there is really no way in which their operations can be examined by the House. This new

House of Commons Procedures committee was added. A Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Development was established to deal with this most important field of activity.

Perhaps the hon. There is a 50 per cent increase in the number of standing committees, and if examined in terms of work envisaged then there will be a like increase in the area of consideration, if I can use that term, upon which the committees will be engaged. But at the same time as we have enlarged the activities of the standing committees-and here is the essential point-we have arranged to refer the estimates of the House of Commons to the committeee so that Members will have an opportunity to examine the administration and expenditures of the various departments.
For that reason, as well as the earlier reason which I gave, we came to the view that it was both premature and unrealistic to add the Committee on Delegated Authority at this time. However, there was no rejection of the idea that the subject matter of delegated authority in any responsible parliament does
2280	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures require better techniques for examination in the years ahead. In other words, there was no repudiation of the idea, but after a good deal of consideration and discussion there was what I might say a rejection of the suggestion that such a standing committee should be provided at time when we are making a rather substantial breakthrough in the whole treatment and structure of committees, with the consequent provision of a tremendous increase in the work to be assigned to them.
I would hope that in light of that explanation the amendment will not be pressed at this time until the Commission on Administrative Tribunals has had an opportunity to report.

Mr. Chairman, I want to rise briefly to say that I support the amendment that has been moved by the hon. Member for Peace River. It seems that the President of the Privy Council is agreeing to it; at least he certainly agreed with the principle that there was a need for the kind of function which this committee would perform.
When the President of the Privy Council began his remarks he said he did not have the committee report before him, but that their report was substantially different from the account given by the hon. Member for Peace River and the hon. Member for Edmonton West. I have in front of me the report and would like to read one short paragraph from it. I think this point was gone over very carefully by the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization, which came to the unanimous decision that this committee should have been included. The report says of the Standing Committee on Delegated Legislation.
The function of this committee would be to act as a "watchdog" over the executive in its use of the powers conferred by statute, with the duty of reporting to Parliament any tendency on the part of the executive to exceed its authority. The committee's terms of reference should exclude it from considering the merits of or the policy behind delegated legislation, but it would be expected to draw the attention of Parliament to any regulations or instruments which impose a charge on public revenues, which confer immunity from challenge in the courts, which have an unauthorized retroactive effect, which reveal unusual or unexpected use of a statutory power, or which otherwise exceed the authority delegated by the parent statute.

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext: What I have before me, Mr. Chairman, is the mimeographed copy of the report which was filed on December 14, so I suppose it appears in Votes and Proceedings at about that time.

speechtext: What is the number of the report?

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
It is the fifteenth report.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I disagree that the function of a Committee on Delegated Authority would be the same as that of an ombudsman. This committee would have no authority whatever to delve into the reason behind policy, as the committee stated in its report. Its purpose would be to see that the authority delegated by Parliament to the Executive or any boards or tribunals or branches of any of the departments is not exceeded by way of regulation, and interpretation of such regulation, beyond that authority granted by the parent statute.
We know, Mr. Chairman, there are certain statutes and amendments to statutes which pass through parliament, to which regulations are later attached. Sometimes the practical application and administration of these statutes is not in accordance with what was intended when they passed through this House. Therefore this committee would have the power to take a very close look at the practical application of the authority, to make sure that it was in accordance with the written word in the statute itself. As far as I can see, that is all there is involved in setting up this committee. It would not consider all the statutes in any one year. It would not even delve into all the statutes of one department in any one year. But it would have the opportunity and power, if you want to call it that, to take certain laws and make sure they were being administered according to the terms of those laws.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, that I think the Executive should confine itself to the authority granted by this Parliament. But that would not be the only function of this Committee on Delegated Authority-namely, the function of being a watchdog over the Executive-because in many cases there is a far greater problem in some body examining what the bureaucracy does with power that is conferred on it by Parliament, which grants it to the Executive and through the Executive to Members in the Civil Service, or to what have been referred to as tribunals. So I think this committee would have quite a different function
June 11. 1965	COMMONS
from the normal investigation into the activities of departmental spending by the standing committees that will look at the estimates, and so on.
Therefore I suggest there is really quite a different kind of function proposed for this committee, and I think the Government should give careful consideration to including it, so there can be a piecemeal, or a statute at a time, if I may put it that way, or a statute by statute examination to make sure that the actual, practical application is in line with that which was intended by Parliament when they passed the statute.

It seems to me that he made a very good case for the argument with which I think most of us agree, namely that we should get away from the old, large, unwieldy, unspecialized committee to which Members were assigned, and attended only in a nominal capacity, in favour of a flexible system of smaller working committees, the membership of which will be made up of Members who have a particular interest in following through that particular aspect of parliamentary work. In pointing out the direction in which we are moving it seems to me that the President of the Privy Council was advancing a very strong argument in favour of the amendment of the hon. Member for Peace River.
The only other thing I wish to say, in view of the reference the President of the Privy Council made to the possibility of our having a parliamentary ombudsman, is that I agree this committee, if set up, would have a very different function from that of the ombudsman. But it does seem to me that if we did establish that office and this committee, the committee might from time to time wish to call before it the ombudsman, in very much the same way that the Public Accounts Committee calls before it the Auditor General, in order to take advantage of the special knowledge in certain aspects of the administration of government which he would have

maintopic: AMENDMENT OF STANDING ORDERS RESPECTING CONDUCT OF BUSINESS

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a very brief word, if I may, on this point. It seems to me that what we are seeking to do here is revise the rules, and not to import a new institution, however desirable that might be. While I am not raising any technical arguments, I think there are a great many of us who would have a great deal of sympathy for the general idea that is behind this amendment. As I understand it, in the British Parliament they have had for many years a committee which looks at regulations to see whether they go beyond the power conferred by statute. That is one thing. That is a very proper function of Members of Parliament, it seems to me, namely to satisfy ourselves that the Executive is not trying to legislate by Order in Council, but is only doing those things by Order in Council which Parliament empowers it to do. That is all the Executive should ever be allowed to do, except in exercising those few minor relics of the prerogative that still exist-and they are very minor nowadays.
But, Mr. Chairman, looking very hastily at the report from which the hon. Member for Medicine Hat just quoted it seems to envisage doing something quite different from that. It seems to envisage examining the way in which some body that was probably perfectly legally and regularly constituted is performing its function. I think a great many of us would want to think quite a while about whether that was the most appropriate way for Parliament to exercise its supervision over the Executive; because under our British system of parliamentary Government and of responsible Government it is the Executive who are responsible for every act of the Executive and for every body set up under the Executive functions, and it is the Ministers who are responsible to this whole House. I have always felt that the greatest merit of our system-and I know that the hon. Member for Port Arthur, who is a great exponent of the American system, will not agree with me; but I hope most hon. Members will-is that

a Committee on Human Rights and a Committee on Crown Corporations. Certainly these were at no time included within the phraseology of committees which were capable of being established under the previous Standing Order.
Something has been said to the effect that we should be patient and wait for the years to go by. It may be because of my great age, Mr. Chairman, but from my experience in the seven or so years I have been here it seems to me that the period of gestation between the time someone gets a gleam in his eye and the 10 or 15 or 20 years it apparently takes to implement the idea in the form of legislation is just too many years for me to have to wait, and I hope there are other Members of the Committee who feel the same way.
I recall that when I came back from war service I tried to rehabilitate myself in a knowledge of the law. In the City of Edmonton I went through the library and looked at the federal and provincial statutes. Then the librarian showed me row after row of volumes with page after page of Orders in Council passed during the course of the war. It would have taken many men studying day and night for years to absorb the knowledge and authority contained in those Orders in Council.
Two or three years ago I had the privilege of serving as Chairman of a small committee which inquired into the Emergency Measures Organization and the War Measures legislation. At that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare was a member of the committee. She asked the Clerk of the Privy Council, I believe, to bring before the Committee some of the Orders in Council dealing with this particular phase and we were told that it would take a truck to bring them all to the committee room.
This is the danger that we face at this time. It is like the old Roman emperor who, in order to comply with custom which compelled him to publish the laws, had them engraved on tablets of stone and then hung so high that no one could read them.

I should like to support the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni. I think there is a good deal more to this than the adding of the word "Indian" to the title. Surely it is time the people of Canada realized that here we face what is undoubtedly the greatest unsolved social problem in Canada. The Indian-Eskimo Association which is probably doing more in
[Mr. BamettJ
its field than any other voluntary association, recently made representations to the Government that a separate department be established to deal with Indian questions and that the whole of this work be separated from the Department of Immigration. The Government has gone some distance in this direction; the department now has two separate branches, each under a deputy minister.
A week or so ago I had a question on the order paper asking what had been spent by the Federal Government on services to Indians in the fields of health, education, welfare and economic development. The answer was interesting. During the fiscal year 1963-64 the Federal Government spent $13 J million on welfare, $3J million on education, $22-Jr million on health services and just $3J million on economic development. Contained in these figures is a good indication, in capsule form, of where we have gone wrong. Surely the only way of reaching a situation where the Indian citizens of Canada can play their part and live their lives with the same possibilities open to them as there are to others, is to make sure they have an economic basis permitting them to pay for the services they require, like the rest of the people of Canada. These figures give us a picture of what has gone wrong in the years gone by. We have been prepared to give the Indians sufficient food and shelter to ensure they will not die from exposure or lack of food- very often-but not enough to permit them to develop to the point at which they can make their own way.
I cannot think of anything better than to set up a committee of parliament which would take the time to meet together with officials of the department and the Minister, and deal in great detail with the problems of the Indians. The Province of Manitoba from which I come, the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and, more recently, the Province of Ontario have all begun to spend a great deal more money and effort on trying to improve both the immediate and the long range conditions of the Indians. We have for the first time an opportunity in the next generation to solve this problem, provided we are prepared to do some new and bold thinking. I wish to join my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni in suggesting that one way of doing this would be to set up a separate committee. Here in the Committee of the Whole when we discuss estimates we spend so much time discussing the immigration

problem that we never have more than a couple of hours in which to discuss the serious question of the Indian population. I do not say this critically; the immigration estimates have rightly come in for lengthy examination during the last 50 years. But I do hope the Government will agree with the proposal now before the committee, and that we can have a committee of this House which will spend the necessary time on this subject and reach the basic solutions which are required.

We all agree in this house that the Indians should have our special attention. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a number of amendments to paragraph 10 in relation to Standing Order 65 by deleting parts of the section and substituting amendments. I do so because I think this is a very important section of the rule changes, one which, in my opinion, can either make them successful or not. I do not want to take up much time by presenting them but I do point out that on a number of things the Government has made certain concessions.
It has been stated that the Government is prepared to have committees established within a ten day period. I should like to move an amendment which provides that after the third day from the commencement of the
June 11. 1965

House of Commons Procedures session a special committee, to consist of seven members, will be automatically established; that within five sitting days after its appointment the committee prepare and lay before the House a list of Members composing the Standing Committees of the House. I would include in the list of committees a subparagraph (b)-I am not opposed to the other recommendations which have been made- a Committee on Accommodation and Facilities, and the Establishment and Organization of the Internal Economy of the House, to consist of 22 Members.
I do not know whether the Government has overlooked this matter, but I think that one of these days we will have to face the problem of the operation of the House itself. I think the way we do it at the moment is pretty archaic. We have a number of treasury members of the Government who, with Mr. Speaker, make decisions as to the operation and establishment of the staff, the facilities, and other matters involving the House. I think any Member who has taken the time to examine the situation will agree that this leaves a great deal to be desired. I think this matter should be considered, and in my opinion will have to be considered, before long.
In the British Parliament, from which many of the recommendations which we have debated over the last few days have been taken, they have established a committee of peers to assist in this matter. The treasury officers and Members of the treasury benches still sit on that committee because obviously an expenditure of money is involved, but it does seem that in Great Britain something can be gained by bringing in other Members of the House to discuss problems affecting the operation of all Members of Parliament and the facilities and establishment of the House of Commons. Therefore I suggest this new committee.
I realize that this will not pass, Mr. Chairman, because Government Members, several of whom are in the House at the present time, are on the presently existing committee. They have had it all their own way for a long time, and without any doubt it is a political committee. So I do not expect support for my amendment.

maintopic: DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
speechtext:
second reading of Bill No. C-3, respecting the national game of Canada (lacrosse).
He said: Mr. Speaker, it may seem from the explanatory notes that this Bill, particularly the portion which reads-
The purpose of this Bill is to rectify what was probably an oversight on the part of the Fathers of Confederation-
-is not seriously intended. This view was probably increased at the time I presented a similar bill last October when there were stories on the sports pages to the effect the Indians might be waiting outside the House to scalp Members who did not support the bill. In spite of remarks of this type, I assure hon. Members the bill is seriously intended.
I think it is fitting at this time when we are considering national flags, national anthems and other national symbols, that this particular matter should be settled now. A few months ago no one thought such a bill was necessary. I am sure they would have assumed that lacrosse was our national game. Reference is made to this in a great many publications. I was looking at one book entitled, "Great Days in Canadian Sport" by Henry Roxborough-I hope you will notice the name of the author-published in 1957. On page 21 this sentence appears:
The game spread so rapidly that in 1867 one of the first Acts approved by the Confederation Parliament was to confirm that Lacrosse was Canada's national game-
There is a book in the Library of Parliament entitled, "Lacrosse and How to Play It", by W. K. McNaught, and reference is made there to Lacrosse as the national game of Canada. I have searched through the Parliamentary Library and in a publication called "The Canadian Magazine" of 1902 there is the following reference:
-on the day on which the different provinces of Canada were united into one grand Dominion- July 1st, 1867-the game Lacrosse was established as the national game of the new Dominion.
June 11, 1965

However, what was assumed was not so. We found that the hon. Member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) caused some research to be done, and this research revealed there could be no record found of any legislative or executive action taken to declare lacrosse to be the national game of Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The purpose of this bill, therefore, is to correct that oversight. I would base my claim for recognition of lacrosse as our official game on two main points. It was played by the Indians a very long time ago. We Canadians have not done too much for the people whose land we took. The least that we can do is to recognize their game as the national game of the country.
The second point we should take into account is the historical fact that lacrosse has long been considered as the national game of Canada. It can probably be proven that more people play hockey and baseball in Canada than lacrosse, but the case for lacrosse should be based upon other considerations. The game is very popular at the moment. It was popular in the past; it suffered a decline, but now there is a revival in its popularity.
The president of the Canadian Lacrosse Association, Mr. Carl Madgett, informs me that there are in excess of 25,000 players in Ontario, 5,000 in Quebec and about 4,500 in B.C. Some lacrosse is played in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, at the University of New Brunswick, and at Camp Gagetown in New Brunswick.
As I have said, there is a considerable revival of interest in the game. It is flourishing in B.C. where there are numerous leagues including teams from Vancouver, New Westminster, Victoria, Burnaby, Coquitlam and Richmond. There are two senior leagues in the Province of Quebec, and the cities of Cornwall and Hull play in the Quebec league.
The National Film Board has just completed a film on lacrosse, which has been released in English and French and is being widely shown throughout the country. Just this past week the Fitness and Amateur Sport Directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare issued a booklet called "Lacrosse" in one of its "How To" series.
We have only to look at the list of the teams which have won the various championships in Canada in past years to see how many parts of the country in which the game is played. The Mann Cup, which is emblematic of the Canadian senior lacrosse championship, was won in recent years by Vancouver, New West-
Lacrosse
minster, Victoria and Nanaimo in B.C. and in Ontario by Port Credit, Peterborough, Hamilton, St. Catharines, Mimico, Brampton, Ottawa, Orillia, and several times by the City of Toronto. The City of Oshawa won the Canadian junior lacrosse championship last year, and the main point I want to get across is that there is great interest in the game at the present time.
In addition to being played widely in this country it is also played in other countries. It is very popular in many parts of the United States, and I understand is the official state game of the State of Maryland. It is also played in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. The Canadian Lacrosse Association hopes to arrange a series of international contests to be played in Canada in 1967, and hopes to invite teams from Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.
It is of particular interest that the only lacrosse equipment factory in the world is situated in Cornwall in the riding which you represent, Mr. Deputy Speaker, the Chisholm Lacrosse Manufacturing Company on the St. Regis reserve near Cornwall.
I expect to get the wide support of the House for this bill. I am sure all Liberal Members will support it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is the honorary president of the Canadian Lacrosse Association, and I believe the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) expressed an interest in the game when he was asked about this by the Canadian Lacrosse Association.
I know a great many Members are interested and will want to speak on the subject, so perhaps my last words on it should be ones which have come from two native Indians. I refer first to a remark made by Mr. Wilfred Pelletier, executive director of the National Indian Council, reported in the Toronto Telegram of November 6, 1964:
Any contribution made by Indians in the past has not received credit, but lacrosse is something we are very proud of, and we of the National Indian Council back the lacrosse associations solidly.
This Parliament can do something to recognize the contribution of Indians by declaring lacrosse our national game.
Another Indian by the name of Duke Red-bird, of Thunderbird Magazine, had this to say:
I can't recall the Russians ever beating a Canadian lacrosse team, or even challenging one.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, there was some humour attached to this when I first intro-
