Lacrosse
duced the bill, and the hon. Member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) introduced a bill dealing with hockey, but so far as I am concerned this bill is quite seriously intended and I should like to see the House take action today to establish this Canadian game as the official game of the country.

maintopic: DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in the debate on Bill No. C-3 to make lacrosse Canada's national game. All the more so because I am honorary president of the Club national de Valleyfield in the Quebec lacrosse league, and I am happy to hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) say a little earlier that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was himself honorary vice president of the Canadian Lacrosse Association.
Mr. Speaker, lacrosse is a game which was very popular at one time in Valleyfield where I live and I am happy to see that this year a group of sportsmen is giving us the opportunity to install new life in this game which is infact traditionally and historically Canadian.
I would feel very remiss indeed if I did not congratulate those who took this happy initiative, among others, people whom you may not know, Mr. Speaker. Mr. J. Gerard Villeneuve and Mr. Bernard "Coco" Blanchard, two very well known sportsmen among our people. And I should not forget either those who will bend every effort throughout the season.
I wish the Valleyfield team good luck. Up to now everything has been going pretty well, and I hope the people will give it all the support required.
To come back to the bill itself, I want to inform the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, if he has not understood the meaning of my remarks, that I support his proposal, and I suggest that all members do the same.
The sponsor of the bill said a while ago that many did not take this suggestion too seriously. As far as I am concerned, I am in earnest. We speak about protecting, even maintaining a sport which originated in Canada, a sport which is becoming more and more popular. In fact, here in the Hull-Ot-tawa area, the newspapers give us each evening the results of various lacrosse games.
Mr. Speaker, I understand very well the reaction of some hon. members who wonder why we insist on having as a national game one which, in the last few years, has been

pushed aside by other games, hockey in particular.
It is also quite understandable that the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh), who was active in amateur hockey for 15 years or so, is not very enthusiastic about this bill, but I hope he will be open minded enough to admit that lacrosse has some claims to being Canada's national game.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-3 is certainly not trying to discredit other sports practiced in Canada today and I am the first to admit that one does not exclude the others. However, one fact remains; lacrosse is of Canadian origin, it is a game older than confederation itself and it was played a long time before the first settlers landed.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to embarrass you, but since lacrosse sticks are manufactured solely in your riding, that is on St. Regis island, I am sure you are in favour of this bill which would be quite normal in my opinion. Besides a great many people know that for many years you have been an avid supporter of lacrosse. That industry in the Cornwall area exports lacrosse sticks tc many countries, mainly to Australia, New Zealand. England and, of course, the United States. Therefore, this sport is renowned internationally; it started in Canada, the sticks are made in Canada and the world's greatest players of lacrosse have always been Canadians. This is significant just the same and I think those are sufficient arguments to make us consider such a sport at a time when we are thinking of adopting a national sport for our country.
If we refer to any encyclopedia, we find at the word lacrosse, that it is "the oldest game played in America" and also "that it is of Canadian origin". The white people started to take an interest in that game around 1840, but the native Indians had played it long before the arrival of the discoverers. It was then called "baggataway", and the teams included between 75 to 200 players. There was no limitation as far as the size of the grounds was concerned, which would extend, in some cases, to five or even ten miles.
Quite obviously, the rules prevailing at that time were completely different from what they are today and the first French settlers were most impressed, both by the game itself and the shape of the stick. Indeed, it is for that very reason that it has been called
June 11. 1965

"lacrosse", on account of the curve at one end, resembling a bishop's staff. The contests were then preceded by elaborate celebrations and religious ceremonies and followed afterwards by a tremendous celebration. The women attending the matches ran along the lines, striking their tribesmen with twigs so as to spur on their players in order to render the action more furious and more thrilling. As for the witch doctors, they acted as referees and marked the limits of the game area but, in some cases, this area could extend further and further as the game went on, since the dividing lines were extended whenever a player went beyond the limits.
On June 4, 1763, a "baggataway" match was used as a means of perpetrating the greatest massacre in Canadian history. According to Mr. J. B. Patterson, the author of "The Black Sparrow-hawk's biography", the Chippewas, a tribe that lived near fort Michillimaekinac, organized a "baggataway" match against the "Sacs" Tribe, in honour of the anniversary of King George III of England, which was celebrated on June 4. The Chief of the Chippewas informed the commander of the fort, Captain Etherington, that a match was being organized in honour of the King's birthday, between his tribe and the "Sacs" tribe. Soldiers and fort visitors were invited to watch the game but the captain was suspicious and refused to let his men leave the precincts. Then, the Indians decided to play the game near the fortress, so that the people inside could watch the game anyway. The game went on for several hours and many soldiers and trappers finally decided to get out of the precincts to come near the ground and watch the competition from closer range. No one had paid too much attention to the fact that the Indian women, contrary to their habit, were sitting on the sideline and were covered with heavy blankets, although it was an extremely hot day. Because of constant coming and going of the fort people, the doors finally remained wide open and suddenly, as the play got nearer and nearer, the signal was given by the Indian chiefs. They all threw away their sticks and hastily picked their tomahawks from under the blankets covering their women. History tells us that only three white men survived that adventure which stands out in our history as one of the worst massacres.
In 1840, when white men began to get interested in the game, they amended the rules and also the stick. Gradually, numerous revisions brought the game to what it 22620-147
Lacrosse
is today. More and more, it is being played indoors with six player teams and although the game may still seem a little rough, we are far from the massacres of 200 years ago. Even if lacrosse can be tough, it is essentially a team sport, a sport of contact, where skill comes first and where little is left to luck. The ball must keep moving at all times and the fact that there are very few offsides makes the game most interesting.
Among the references I found, some say that lacrosse was selected as the national sport of Canada in 1867, but after checking I found that nothing in the statutes of our country indicates that parliament ever took such a decision. Therefore I consider that the bill introduced today by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond is more than justified, because it will enable us to recognize and preserve a sport which could not be more Canadian and which we could easily develop and make popular.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I invite all hon. members to support Bill No. C-3 and to recognize in lacrosse a sport which was marked by Canadian destiny and must remain with us, not like any other sport, but rather as the national sport of Canada.

speechtext:
I wish to speak briefly in support of the bill sponsored by my hon. friend from Burnaby-Richmond, an area in British Columbia which has a long tradition of lacrosse.
We have heard a great deal in recent years about the need to develop in Canada a Canadian identity as we approach our centennial year. With this in mind we have become increasingly aware of our achievements as a nation in various fields of activity such as resource development, scientific research, the creative arts and international affairs. Last year for the first time in our history we adopted a distinctive Canadian flag. Very soon we shall have an official anthem. Surely the time is ripe for us to recognize our national game of lacrosse.
I suggest there are three reasons why we should make this decision. First, lacrosse was developed many years ago by native people on the northern part of this continent. By accepting lacrosse as Canada's national game we would be paying tribute to the men and women who occupied this land before the coming of the white man. Second, early in this century, lacrosse was considered Canada's

June 11, 1965
Lacrosse
No. 1 game, with widespread interest in both professional and amateur leagues. One of my first boyhood heroes was Newsy Lalonde -a great French athlete who played professional lacrosse for Vancouver and hockey for Montreal. The third reason is that lacrosse is a good game for Canadian youth. It requires skill, stamina and sportsmanship of a high order. We should give it official recognition.
In conclusion, I wish to quote an editorial from the Ottawa Journal of May 15, entitled "Lively Lacrosse". It reads as follows:
Occasional claims that lacrosse Is Canada's national sport have not met wide public acceptance in recent years. Most people know that the game has a colourful Canadian history dating back to days when Indians ruled the land. In those times, it was played by 75 to 200 braves using a curved webbed stick that eventually was to give lacrosse its name-the stick reminded French settlers of a bishop's crozier, hence "La crosse."
Great changes occurred in the game after white men took a fancy to it...fewer players and smaller playing areas were introduced, until today it can be played in a hockey arena. The Mann Cup is the prize for national supremacy in the sport, which resembles hockey in its strategy.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Ottawa has harboured many avid lacrosse players over the years and both this city and Hull have entries in the Quebec League this year. The Ottawa-Montreal-Comwall area appears to be a growing centre for the sport, which offers rugged action and high scores to please spectators.
Whether lacrosse, or any other sport, should be declared the national game is a matter of controversy. But lacrosse certainly deserves a better fate than the all-too-common one of being airily dismissed by people who have never seen the game played!

maintopic: DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to this debate will not be very significant; besides, I speak with a certain apprehension, especially after hearing the favourable remarks made by some members and colleagues.
I wish at first to congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) who introduced bill No. C-3 to have lacrosse declared our national game, not for having chosen this one but to have had the idea of having a game recognized as our national sport, a thing we should do as soon as possible. He gave us also a very interesting historical background about this sport which was played by our native Indian people, our predecessors, or shall I say, the first Canadians. He gave us also an historical account of what has happened since the adoption of the game by Canadians.

I have no resentment against the Indians, Mr. Speaker, but I remember very well- I still have the marks on my body-the first time I played lacrosse as a student at the Oka school. I then had the opportunity of playing against the Indians of Caughna-waga. It was a worthwhile personal experience but it nevertheless left me with a few scars which will show for some time yet.
I agree, as I mentioned earlier, that Canada should adopt a national sport, but I wonder if lacrosse should be the one to be so designated. I readily understand that lacrosse has been played from time immemorial and that it is also very popular here in Canada and elsewhere. On the other hand, I do not think lacrosse should be recognized as our national sport because I feel that a national sport should be practiced by most sportsmen. I also feel that it should promote national interest in times of national competition. Lacrosse does not qualify in this respect, no matter how it is compared to hockey.
Hockey is played by hundreds of thousands of people in Canada; it is governed by a national organization and millions of fans follow it. I feel that hockey qualifies much better as our national sport than lacrosse. Furthermore, national radio and television networks spend a great deal of money to broadcast hockey games and there is organized hockey in every Canadian community, be it a large city or a humble village.
Therefore, in my opinion, if we must recognize a national sport-and in this I share the opinion of the Member for Burnaby-Richmond-hockey wins by a long stretch over lacrosse, against which I hold no grudge. On the contrary, it is a game which requires a certain robust training, which develops the team spirit, which has great merit and demands considerable effort. However, I do not think it has the necessary qualifications to be designated as our national sport.
Once again, I congratulate the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond for his interest in the selection or designation of a national sport for Canada, and I also congratulate the hon. member for Beauhamois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) for making a worthy contribution to the debate, for doing his best to present all the advantages of the game of lacrosse. However, we are still a long way from adopting that game as our national sport.
Once more, I have no regret in not sharing the opinion of my colleague from Burnaby-Richmond. A referendum to determine which
June 11, 1965

is our most popular sport, what sport mostly attracts players, sportsmen and the general public, will reveal that hockey is our national sport.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a lew words in support of the bill which has been advanced by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie). In other words, I should like to support lacrosse as Canada's national game.
Lacrosse has several things to recommend it. First, historically it comes ahead of ice hockey. It was played in this country generations before ice hockey was invented. Second, it is a tough game. It is a game which calls for a great deal of stamina and skill. Any of you who have seen lacrosse played in recent years will realize that this is indeed a fine game. It is very fast. The ball, for example, never goes out of bounds. The shots on goal are much faster than the shots in ice hockey. The plays are much more intricate. They call for a great deal of skill in respect to stick handling and they are well worth watching, drawing large crowds where the sport has been played continuously over the years. My advocacy of lacrosse, in other words, is based firstly on historical reasons, and secondly on the nature of the game itself.
In respect to historical reasons I would refer very briefly to the Encyclopedia Canadiana, which says that lacrosse is the oldest organized sport in America. It is Canadian in origin. A form of lacrosse, called battagaway, was played by Indian teams of from 75 to 200 men before white men arrived in Canada. As many as 48 tribes or groups, separated by distances up to 3,000 miles-in other words, right across the breadth of this continent, across what is now known as Canada-participated in these events. The game received its present name from early French settlers who likened the curved webbed stick used by the Indians to the bishop's crozier-hence "la crosse".
As early as 1840 white men became interested in lacrosse. It became popular around the middle of the last century. The rules were drawn up with some finality in 1867; in other words, in the year of Canada's birth as a nation. In the 1870's, 1880's and 1890's lacrosse was played by many more Canadians than played ice hockey. In the 1920's, and more particularly in the 1930's, the game was al-
Lacrosse
tered in several important ways. It became necessary, in order to have large attendances, to play on smaller courts. The summer use of ice hockey arenas was one obvious way not only of seating large crowds but of having a facility which could be lighted at night. Wire mesh was strung around the ice hockey arena to keep the ball in bounds. The same area was used as was normally covered by ice. The size of the team was reduced from 12 to 7, in the 1930's. Within the last few years it has been reduced to six. The players, playing in rotation, are substituted much as they are in ice hockey. It therefore is not only a fast game in spots, but it is played continuously at a very high rate of speed with much the same drive and purpose as ice hockey.
Today we have teams right across Canada. Lacrosse is more popular in Ontario than in other parts of the country; but it is certainly played in Quebec and it is played extensively out in British Columbia. This is witnessed by the fact that several Members from British Columbia have spoken today. Also the New Westminster Salmonbellies and the North Shore Indians teams are among the best teams that the nation has ever had. I mention the North Shore partly because the Squamish Indians, who made up the membership of some of our strongest west coast teams, are among the finest players that the Canadian game of lacrosse has ever known. These teams, the Salmonbellies from New Westminster and the North Shore Indians from Coast-Capilano won the Canadian senior men's championship a number of times.
By contrast ice hockey has a relatively recent history. Also its history, according again to several encyclopedias, began in western Europe. It was played in various forms and under various names through the Middle Ages on the canals in Holland, the frozen ponds in Denmark and the British Isles. It was popularly known as the game of "Shinny" for some time. It really was not played in Canada to any great extent until after 1867; hence it post-dates lacrosse by a considerable period of time. It has, however, become much more popular in recent years. This is partly because of the fact that there is a considerable commercial interest in ice hockey, an interest which has spread beyond the Canadian borders into the United States and elsewhere, and many young players are encouraged to improve themselves in this game. Many facilities have become available for the training and development of ice hockey players. I am

June 11, 1965
Lacrosse
personally convinced that in time the improved equipment that is available now to young boys, teen-agers, in respect of ice hockey will also become available in respect of lacrosse. I think many of the new facilities which have been developed for ice hockey will also eventually be used for lacrosse in the late spring, summer and fall months. I believe that with these improved facilities lacrosse may revive, and indeed I believe should revive because it is a fine participators sport and a fine spectator sport.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer briefly to the breakdown of the grants which have been made available to national organizations by the federal department through the good offices of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am referring more particularly to the fiscal year 1963-64. There lacrosse is well down the list. Ice hockey, as represented by the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association, is at the top of the list. No. 2 is the Canadian Amateur Ski Association. No. 3, I notice, is the Canadian Lawn Tennis Association, and No. 4 is the Canadian Association of Amateur Oarsmen. No doubt some of these expenditures reflect the fact that our athletes have excelled themselves in recent years in certain fields. Certainly out in British Columbia we have excelled ourselves in respect of rowing, and hence the amateur oarsmen have moved well up the list. But I suggest that for the Lacrosse Association to receive a mere $5,000 over a two-year period, in contrast to the literally hundreds of thousands of dollars spent in support of other athletic activities, is not doing justice to our national game. I trust that this situation will be rectified and that in view of the growth potential as well as the historical importance of this game it will receive more support from the Canadian Government in the years ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing one of the most sports-minded constituencies in Canada, I feel that I am obliged, indeed that I have a moral obligation to participate in this debate.
Before designating a sport as national,
1 suggest we should consider the criteria on which such a decision should be based. To my mind, there are four possible criteria.
First, the historic origin of the sport. From this standpoint, previous speakers convinced me that lacrosse was older still than

hockey and, therefore, I am ready to concede this first point.
Second, there is the criterion of the value of a sport. I think we should not indulge in a debate in this regard, since each of us will find in his favorite sports a value, a beauty that others will deny. Therefore, the second criterion, in my opinion, does not apply.
There is a third criterion. The popularity of the sport. From that point of view, I think everybody will agree that, at least for the time being, hockey is the most popular sport in Canada and it is more generally practised than the game of lacrosse. In fact, one has only to read the newspapers to find that out.
The game of lacrosse, at least in the province of Quebec, has declined for quite a long time. I admit that recently there was a revival and that it is played more and more. In Drummondville, a city which I have the honour to represent, the game of lacrosse is really spreading and the public is showing greater interest.
There is a fourth criterion which I think is interesting and important, namely the reputation enjoyed by the sport abroad. In that regard, all those who have travelled outside Canada know very well that the game of lacrosse is not considered by the rest of the world as a distinctively Canadian sport. Whether we like it or not, hockey is considered in all countries of the world as Canada's national sport. And that is precisely one of the reasons why we feel so humiliated when the teams representing us in international competitions or at the Olympics are defeated by other countries, precisely because, for the rest of the world, hockey is the first Canadian sport.
There is another aspect to this problem which, I believe, is worth pointing out. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) himself, in the second paragraph of his notes, mentioned a very special aspect of this problem, that is its constitutional aspect. I quote the second paragraph:
The purpose of this bill is to rectify what was probably an oversight on the part of the Fathers of Confederation who were so preoccupied with drafting Sections 91 and 92 of the B.N.A. Act that the question of declaring a national game escaped their attention.
Actually, I am wondering whether or not the Fathers of Confederation did not study this problem very seriously. I admit that history does not report any such discussion, at least to my knowledge, but I feel that the Fathers of Confederation must have consid-
June 11, 1S65

ered this question and, precisely while considering sections 91 and 92, they certainly wondered in which category of problems, federal or provincial, this question of a national game should be included. I suppose some of them referred to section 91(f) as dealing with the defence of the country and I presume it was said that muskets were likely more useful than the lacrosse sticks and, consequently, the possibility was eliminated. Others may have argued this question came under paragraph 22 of section 91 concerning letters patent; others may have said that it pertained to paragraph 23 of section 91 concerning copyrights. Others may have stated that paragraph 24 of section 91 was applicable since the matter came under the jurisdiction of the federal government concerning Indian affairs. But I suppose that the supporters of the federal jurisdiction were themselves a little shaken by the arguments put forward by their opponents.
I suppose that in 1867 some of the Fathers of Confederation said that this decision concerning the national game should, on the contrary, come under the provisions of section 92, and that someone argued that that was provided for in paragraph 13 of section 92 dealing with property and civil rights. I also imagine that some people said this matter came under section 92(7) relating to local matters and consequently is under the provincial jurisdiction.
I can very well imagine that one of the Fathers of Confederation pointed out that weather conditions varied considerably across Canada and that mentalities and temperaments varied also. Furthermore, some must have thought it preferable not to designate any national sport, precisely because one sport could be very popular in one part of the country but less in another.
But, Mr. Chairman, I think there must have been one Father of the Confederation to suggest, finally, that the problem should be examined in the light of section 91 concerning peace and order and the good administration of the country.
One of them must have said: "That is the type of thing which will cause such serious problems between Canadians that it is much better not to raise it at this time. Since some Fathers of Confederation were, in 1867, already concerned about urgency, I imagine that there were some who said that it was not urgent to decide one way or another.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the debate which has just taken place proves that
Lacrosse
even today, almost a century after 1867, we do not agree on what is the national sport of Canada. And I imagine that in the interest of order, peace and good administration, it would be better not to take a decision on this matter today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) who introduced the bill has certainly caused a very interesting discussion on something about which I have heard very little before. Even if he is not successful in having lacrosse established as Canada's national game, he has acquired at least one new fan for that sport.
From what we have heard today, I do not think any of us can dispute the historical significance of the game of lacrosse. The promoter of the bill and the hon. Member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), and others who have spoken, have established beyond any reasonable doubt that lacrosse has been played in this country for a great many years. In fact, as the bill indicates, it has been played in Canada for an unknown period of time, having originated with the native Indian people. On the basis of what has been said by other hon. Members who have spoken I would also agree that lacrosse is certainly an excellent game, one in which stamina, skill, team spirit and active participation are required.
However, in order to establish any sport as the national game I think there are certain other factors that must be taken into consideration in addition to historical background and the fact that lacrosse has many excellent features. I believe that one of the most important factors is that the people of the country would have to accept and recognize lacrosse as the national game, and in my opinion the vast majority of our people would be very reluctant to affirm that this is so.
I know that in my part of the country and probably throughout the whole of the Maritime Provinces the game is not played at all, or at least to a very limited extent at some of the universities. I have never seen an actual game of lacrosse and I think many of my hon. friends from that part of Canada are probably in the same boat. Therefore I would say that by an Act of Parliament we cannot impose on the people of Canada as their national game a game in which very few of them participate, a game which is known to a very small number of Canadians.

11 June, 1965.
Statement by the Minister of Finance on the Canada Student Loans Plan
When I reported on the Canada Student Loans Plan to the House last November, about 29,000 students had then been assisted by means of Canada Student Loans in the first two months of the new program. Total loans authorized at that time amounted to about $20 million. Since then, students have continued to make good use of this Plan and according to the latest figures available, as of April 1, 1965, over 41,000 students had been issued Certificates of Eligibility by the provincial authorities for a total amount of some $26 million. This means that the actual utilization of allocations by participating provinces during the current loan year will be quite close to the total provided for in the Act.
In my last statement I explained that, after the Plan had been in operation for a few months, it became apparent that a number of administrative problems encountered by the participating provinces were the result of varying practices in handling student aid, and that a concerted effort was being made to seek a greater degree of harmony in these practices. To this end, provincial officials and officials of the Department of Finance have met on several occasions during recent months to work out a common approach to these administrative problems.
The problems fall into three categories: the principles and criteria which the provincial authorities should apply in determining the size of loan (if any) which the student needs; the standard residence rules to be used in determining the province to which students should apply for Certificates of Eligibility; and, finally, questions relating to the designation by the provinces of educational institutions and related matters.
The federal-provincial representatives have prepared reports on each of the three areas I have mentioned. These reports have been accepted recently by a full federal-provincial meeting, at which representatives of all participating provinces and the federal government were present.
Because of the responsibilities which the provinces have assumed in the implementation of the Plan, these reports deal primarily with aspects of the student loan program which fall within the jurisdiction of the Provincial administrators. Indeed, the understandings reached in each of these reports reflect the experience and expertise of provincial authorities in the field of student assistance. I would like to express my appreciation to the representatives of all the provinces and territories for their efforts. The application of these reports will, I feel sure, make a major contribution to the effectiveness of this student aid program, and I can affirm that the reports carry the full support of the federal government.
The first report deals with the difficult question of how best to administer the provision of the Act which requires that the Certificate of Eligibility issued to a student should indicate that "the student is considered to be in need of a student loan for the academic year ... in order to pursue a course of studies." We have learned from experience this year that a reasonably standard approach to this question is highly desirable, if not essential. It is in the general interests of the Plan to ensure that the available funds are utilized to assist only those students who genuinely need assistance. This means that the provincial administrators need guidelines to ensure that student needs will be measured in much the same way in all participating provinces. Also, a standard approach is needed to provide more concrete guidance to students in submitting their loan applications.
In considering the question of the financial needs of students, it is assumed that responsibility for the costs of post-secondary education of the individual student remains primarily with the parent or family of dependant students, or with the student himself where he is not a dependant. It is also recognized, however, that governments at all levels are interested in supplementing their available resources in order to ensure that all qualified students have the opportunity to reach their educational potential. These premises are set out in detail in the report.

June 11, 1965
It follows from these premises that, as a general rule, the parents' income should be taken into account in assessing a student's need for a loan. The report therefore spells out in some detail how a student's need is to be determined, taking into account both the costs of continuing his education and the financial resources that are available to him. However, the report also provides for an appeal procedure where an applicant feels that this assessment is inadequate or where the circumstances have changed since the application was first made. The applicant may, in these circumstances, re-apply or appeal his case, in accordance with the policies of the provinces concerned. I think that this is a very important feature and I am confident that, as a result, a loan will be made to any student who really needs a loan, and who meets the other requirements.
Provincial officials and representatives of the Department of Finance will be meeting again next week with the objective of ensuring the implementation of these criteria as uniformly as possible in all participating provinces.
The second report on questions of residence establishes the principles to be used in determining which province is the appropriate one to handle a student's application. Participating provinces are, as a matter of policy, issuing Certificates only to their own residents. However, with a mobile population- and an even more mobile student body-the question of residence can be complicated and controversial. Initially, provinces did not apply the same definition of residence, so that some students experienced difficulty in having their application considered by what they thought was the appropriate province. The report establishes agreement among the participating provinces on full reciprocity in the application of the same residence definitions. In addition, it has been agreed that the ultimate goal is to have complete reciprocity on
the question of residence with the Province of Quebec, which does not participate in the federal Plan.
I am glad to mention that the student-aid authorities in Quebec participated fully in working out the common guidelines, and their experience in operating their own program of student aid was of considerable help to the other members of these committees.
The third report deals with a number of miscellaneous but nevertheless important subjects such as the criteria for designation of educational institutions, definitions of what is meant by "post-secondary" school level, "Satisfactory scholastic standard" and "academic year". The understandings that have been reached will serve to assure equitable and standard rules in all the provinces.
This report does not deal with the question of what type or types of private schools, if any, should be eligible for designation by a province as a "specified educational institution" within the meaning of the Act. This is a difficult subject and is still under active consideration. As soon as agreement has been reached, it will be announced.
The principles and procedures reflected in these three reports should come into effect starting with the new loan year which begins in July. As I have said earlier, they can be expected to contribute significantly in making the operation of the Plan more effective and equitable, and should help to ensure that all Canadian students who genuinely need assistance to finance their education will obtain it.
The high degree of success which this Plan has enjoyed is due to a large extent to the constructive spirit of cooperation of the provinces and territories, and the lending agencies. The Plan was initiated shortly before the beginning of the academic year last Fall. It is to the credit of the provincial authorities administering the Plan that it was possible to implement it so quickly and so effectively.

Approved Report of the Federal-Provincial Standing Committee on Concept of Students' Need
1. The premises on which the concepts of need are based include the following:-
(a)	The responsibility for the costs of postsecondary education to the individual student remains primarily with the parent (guardian or immediate family) where the student is a dependant or with the student where he is not a dependant.
(b)	Governments at all levels are interested in supplementing family/student resources and resources available through educational institutions, where needed to ensure that all qualified students have the opportunity to reach their educational potential.
(c)	It is desirable that the concepts and criteria used by governments and institutions in determining the need for loans, bursaries and other forms of assistance to students should be co-ordinated within a province by a provincial authority.
(d)	It is possible to co-ordinate among the provinces the concepts and criteria of need applied in administering federal assistance in this field.
2. Both the costs of education and resources available to the student should be taken into account in developing the concepts of need.
The following criteria should be employed:
A.	Costs of Education The following costs should be taken into account in determining need:

June 11, 1965
(1)	Fees-All compulsory fees of the educational institution.
(2)	Prescribed Books and Instruments.
(3)	Board and Lodging During the Academic Year Single Students.
(i)	Institutional Residence-as charged by the institution.
(ii)	Board and lodging away from home, based on average costs in the region concerned.
(iii)	Students living at home will be given an allowance against student resources.
Married Students: Board and lodging allowance in accordance with the rate for a single student established as above may be allowed for each married student attending an institution. (A reasonable amount will be deductible from the financial resources of a married student (B below) to reflect the additional costs of maintaining a household.)
(4)	A Reasonable Allowance for Clothing, Laundry, Dry-Cleaning and Recreational Costs.
(5)	Transportation: (a) From permanent residence in Canada to institution in Canada: One return trip a year, the cost not to exceed the equivalent of the cost of the most economical means based on costs of public transportation.
(b)	From permanent residence in Canada to institution outside of Canada: An allowance which will equal the lesser of one return trip a year by the most economical transportation, or a maximum amount established by the provinces.
(c)	A reasonable allowance for Local Transportation.
(6)	Premiums for Hospital and Medical Prepayment Plans.
B.	Student Financial Resources
(1)	Resources of Parents/Guardian: Parents' personal taxable income including income on assets are factors to be taken into account, and will be shown in application forms unless the student is married or can establish that he is completely independent financially from his parents/guardian.
(2)	Students' Own Resources: (a) Summer Earnings; (b) Assets.
(i)	Car (state value); (ii) Other Assets.
(c)	Earnings During the Academic Year;
(d)	Scholarships, Bursaries and Tuition Grants.
(3)	Spouse's Gross Income
3.	General Recommendations: (1) Where an applicant feels that the award is inadequate or circumstances have changed since
the award was made, the applicant may reapply or appeal his case in accordance with the policy of the province concerned. In all participating provinces, except Ontario, such re-application or appeal is to be made to the provincial authority; in Ontario, it is to be made to the institution attended if located within the province, or to the Provincial Authority for Ontario residents studying outside Ontario.
(2)	A declaration shall be made by the student in his application of the same force and effect as if made under oath by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act, and where applicable by the parent/guardian.
(3)	These premises and criteria are acceptable to provincial and federal governments, and the federal and all provincial authorities will co-operate in giving full publicity to them.
4.	Continuing attention will be given to developing a common application form for use in the provinces.
The above report was accepted on March 29, 1965, by a full federal-provincial meeting, including representatives of all participating provinces and the federal government.

Approved Report of the Federal-Provincial Committee on Residence
(I)	Criteria for Determination of Issuing Province for students from Participating Provinces (Except as in (II) Below)
A distinction is made between
Group A: Unmarried students who receive financial support from parents, guardians or foster parents; and
Group B: Students who are married or who can establish to the satisfaction of the Appropriate Authority or its agent that they are completely independent financially.

In the case of Group A, a student's Issuing Province is:
(a)	the province where his parents, guardians or foster parents reside; or
June 11, 1965

(b)	the province where his family's home is being maintained, even if one of his parents works in another province; or
(c)	if parents are separated or divorced, the province where that parent (father or mother) resides with whom the student normally lives or from whom he receives his principal financial support if he lives with neither; or
(d)	if parents, guardians or foster parents live abroad (e.g., armed services), the province where they last lived before going abroad.
Where the persons whose residence determines a student's Issuing Province move to another province, the province to which they have moved becomes the student's new Issuing Province as of the date of the move.

In the case of Group B, a student establishes residence in his own right. For Group B students, however, there will be a time lag of not less than 12 consecutive months before residence is established in a new province. A participating province continues to be the Issuing Province of a student in Group B who leaves that province, until the student has spent 12 consecutive months in another participating province which latter province then becomes the Issuing Province.

A landed immigrant who has been in Canada for one year or more, but who does not qualify for residence in a participating province as outlined above, may be considered to be a resident in the participating province in which he lives when applying for a Certificate.
If a student's application for a Certificate is refused on the grounds that he is not a resident of the province to which he applied, his application will be redirected to his province of origin.
(II) Pro Tern Criteria for the Determination of Issuing Province for Students in the Case of Moves in Either Direction Between a Participating Province and a Non-Participating Province
The objective as regards residence criteria is complete reciprocity between participating and non-participating provinces. Pending further consultation between Quebec and the participating provinces, the latter are prepared to proceed on the following basis:
(i)	If the parents, guardians or foster parents of an unmarried student receiving financial support from them, or if students who are married or who have established that they are
completely independent financially, move from a participating province to the Province of Quebec, the Province of Issue prior to the move remains the Province of Issue of these students until they qualify for student assistance from the Province of Quebec under that province's residence rules.
(ii) In the case of a student moving from Quebec to a participating province, that participating province will apply the same residence criteria as if the student came from a participating province.

The above report was accepted on March 29, 1965, by a full federal-provincial meeting, including representatives of all participating provinces and the federal government.

Ottawa, Ontario.

Approved Report of Federal-Provincial Committee on Designation of Educational Institutions and Related Definitions
1.	Criteria for Designation of Educational Institutions.
The Act provides that student loans are intended for students taking courses at a postsecondary school level. Accordingly, it is agreed that post-secondary educational institutions, including such institutions outside Canada, be designated by the individual provinces on the basis of academic entrance requirements and course content.
It is further agreed that no course or institution be designated if the requirements for entrance to the course or institution are below the level generally accepted in the designating province as complete high school.
2.	Private Educational Institutions.
[An agreed text to be incorporated later.]
3.	Post-Secondary School Level of Course or Courses.
This means a course of study provided by specified educational institutions for which the generally accepted entrance requirements

June 11, 1965
include the successful completion of high school in the designating province.
4.	Satisfactory Scholastic Standard.
A student who is accepted for enrolment by a designated institution in an approved course may be considered by a provincial authority to have achieved a "satisfactory scholastic standard".
5.	Definition of Academic Year (Trimester and Semester).
Where an academic year overlaps two loan years the student, on the initial application, may be granted only that amount of loan required to finance the portion of the course which will be completed during the first loan year and instructed to re-apply for the amount required to finance the portion of the academic year which occurs during the second loan year. It is understood that the combined loans in a single academic year will not exceed $1,000.
The present legislation does not take into account the additional needs of students who
attend institutions operating on the trimester system, since such students are limited to loans of $1,000 per academic year, even though the course of studies takes approximately one year less than a similar course taken at another institution. It is suggested that this question be re-considered when the Act is being reviewed.
The above report was accepted on March 29, 1965, by a full federal-provincial meeting, including representatives of all participating provinces and the federal government.
